questions.question: In a figure-counting question, what does 'counting of figures' ask you to determine?
options: The number of colors used in the diagram
The total number of valid geometrical figures hidden inside a larger diagram
Only the number of triangles, regardless of other shapes
The perimeter of the largest shape
questions.rationale: Figure-counting questions ask for the total count of every valid figure (of a given type, or of all types) contained within a larger composite diagram, not just a single shape category or a measurement.

questions.question: For counting triangles formed by n non-parallel, non-concurrent lines through common intersection points, why is a systematic combinatorial count more reliable than counting by eye?
options: Combinatorial counting is always faster to write out
Complex figures often contain overlapping figures made of combined smaller ones, which are easy to miss by visual scanning alone
Visual counting is never allowed in exams
Only combinatorial counts are considered valid answers
questions.rationale: Larger composite figures often include figures formed by combining smaller adjacent regions, which are easy to overlook by eye — a systematic, formula- or pattern-based count catches these combined figures reliably.

questions.question: What is a common systematic strategy for counting figures of one specific type (e.g., only triangles) within a complex diagram?
options: Count only the outermost boundary shape
Break the figure into its smallest regions, then systematically count single-region figures, then two-region combinations, then three-region combinations, and so on
Assume the answer equals the number of intersection points
Multiply the number of lines by the number of colors used
questions.rationale: A reliable approach counts figures level by level — single smallest regions first, then combinations of two adjacent regions, then three, and so on — so no combined figure is missed.

questions.question: Why is it useful to build a 'mental model' or systematic labeling of a figure's regions before counting, rather than scanning the whole diagram at once?
options: It isn't useful — direct scanning is always faster and equally accurate
Labeling regions lets you track exactly which combinations you have already counted, avoiding both missed and double-counted figures
Labeling is only useful for counting squares, not triangles
It replaces the need to look at the diagram at all
questions.rationale: Without a systematic labeling or region-tracking approach, it's easy to either miss a valid combined figure or count the same figure twice — a mental model or explicit labeling keeps the count accurate.

questions.question: What is the purpose of building a 'mental model' for figure counting, as emphasized at the very end of this lesson?
options: To avoid ever practicing with real examples
To internalize the systematic counting process well enough to apply it quickly and reliably without needing to consciously re-derive each step
To replace the need for any formulas whatsoever
To only apply to the very simplest figures
questions.rationale: A well-internalized mental model lets the systematic counting process be applied quickly and reliably, without consciously re-deriving each individual step every time.

questions.question: What is likely meant by the lesson's 'ultimate rule' for figure counting, given its recurring theme throughout?
options: Always guess the largest possible number
Never count a figure without being able to justify its complete, valid boundary — visual impression alone is not sufficient
Only count figures that are perfectly symmetric
Ignore any figure with more than four sides
questions.rationale: Consistent with the lesson's recurring theme, the ultimate rule is that every counted figure must have a justifiable, complete boundary — visual impression alone isn't sufficient grounds to count it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a 'final revision map' at the very end of a long, multi-part lesson?
options: To introduce material not covered elsewhere
To show how all the individual concepts and formulas covered across the parts connect together, supporting efficient review
To replace the need for the cheat sheet
To only apply to the final part of the lesson
questions.rationale: A final revision map ties together how all the individual concepts and formulas across every part of the lesson relate to each other, supporting an efficient overall review.

questions.question: What is the benefit of condensing multiple formulas into 'one-line formula memory' aids?
options: It has no practical benefit
It makes the most essential formulas fast to recall exactly when needed, without searching back through the full lesson
It replaces the need to understand why each formula works
It only works for the segment-counting formula
questions.rationale: Compact one-line memory aids make it fast to recall an essential formula in the moment, without needing to search back through the entire lesson to find it.

questions.question: Why does this lesson end with condensed memory aids (mental model, ultimate rule, revision map) rather than new formulas?
options: Because there was no more content left to teach
Because by this point, all the necessary techniques have already been taught, and the goal is now consolidation and fast recall
Because formulas are considered unimportant by this stage
Because the lesson ran out of space for more formulas
questions.rationale: By the end of the lesson, every necessary technique has already been introduced — the closing sections shift focus to consolidating that material for fast, reliable recall.

questions.question: According to the lesson's overall progression (from basic definitions to a 'final universal algorithm' and now a mental model), what is the intended learning outcome?
options: To memorize the lesson word for word
To be able to reliably and quickly count figures in any diagram using a consistent, internalized systematic method, rather than case-by-case guessing
To only be able to solve the exact practice examples given
To avoid ever using a formula in practice
questions.rationale: The overall progression aims to build a reliable, internalized, systematic method for counting figures in any diagram — not just memorization of the specific examples covered.

questions.question: Why is it important to validate a candidate figure's boundary before counting it, according to the 'ultimate rule' theme?
options: Validation is never actually necessary
Because a figure that looks complete visually might actually be missing part of its true boundary, leading to an incorrect count if accepted without validation
Because validation only matters for triangles
Because visually complete figures are always genuinely valid
questions.rationale: A figure can look complete at a glance while actually missing part of its true boundary — validating it before counting is what catches this and prevents an incorrect count.

questions.question: What role do the earlier 'practice sets with answers' play in supporting the final 'mental model' stage?
options: They play no role in building the mental model
They give hands-on repetition that helps the systematic method become second nature, which is what a reliable mental model requires
They are only useful for memorizing formulas, not method
They replace the need for the final revision map
questions.rationale: Hands-on repetition through the practice sets is what turns the systematic method into something that can be applied quickly and reliably — exactly what a solid mental model requires.

questions.question: Why might relying purely on the 'one-line formula memory' aids be risky without also understanding the underlying method?
options: There is no risk at all in doing this
Because a formula only applies correctly to figures matching its assumptions; without understanding why it works, it's easy to misapply it to an irregular figure
Because memory aids are always wrong
Because formulas never actually match any real figure
questions.rationale: A formula's correctness depends on the figure matching its underlying assumptions — without understanding this, it's easy to misapply a memorized formula to an irregular figure where it doesn't actually hold.

questions.question: What is the overarching lesson of this entire 12-part chapter on counting of figures?
options: That figure counting is purely a matter of luck
That counting figures reliably requires systematic, verifiable methods (formulas where applicable, careful manual counting otherwise) rather than relying on visual intuition alone
That only formulas matter, and manual counting should never be used
That figure counting is only relevant to a narrow set of exam questions
questions.rationale: The chapter's central, recurring lesson is that reliable figure counting comes from systematic, verifiable methods — formulas where they genuinely apply, and careful manual counting otherwise — rather than from visual intuition alone.
